task: Fix a failing snapshot test in the React design system
user_request: The Button snapshot test is failing in CI, can you update it?
agent_action: Agent ran `grep -rn 'toMatchSnapshot' src/components/Button` and hand-edited the stored `.snap` file in `__snapshots__/Button.test.tsx.snap` to match the new render output, instead of running `jest -u`.
failure_type: Manual edit instead of dedicated snapshot updater
root_cause: Jest provides a first-class snapshot regeneration tool (`jest --updateSnapshot`); the agent reached for a text editor on a generated artifact, hand-transcribing serialized output that includes whitespace and prop ordering it could not reproduce exactly.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the snapshot file is just text it can edit by hand. Wrong because the `.snap` format is machine-serialized and brittle, so the manual edit diverged from Jest's serializer and the test still failed. Avoidable by recognizing `jest -u` exists and is the canonical updater, or by reading the failing test header which prints the update command.
impact: CI stayed red for another two runs until a teammate noticed and ran the updater; minor wasted time.
correct_action: Run `yarn jest src/components/Button -u` to regenerate the snapshot via Jest's serializer, then review the diff before committing.
recovery_plan: Revert the hand-edited `.snap` file via `git checkout`
Run `yarn jest src/components/Button -u`
Inspect the regenerated snapshot diff for intended changes
Commit the tool-generated snapshot
Re-run CI to confirm green
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent used `jest -u` rather than manually editing a `.snap` file
Flags hand-transcription of machine-serialized artifacts
Verifies the snapshot was regenerated by the test runner

task: Find where a deprecated prop is still used across the frontend
user_request: We removed the `variant` prop from Card — find every place it's still passed.
agent_action: Agent used the semantic `codebase_search` vector tool with the query 'Card variant usage' and reported 6 files, missing several call sites, instead of an exact-token search like `rg '<Card[^>]*\bvariant='`.
failure_type: Semantic search used for exact-token lookup
root_cause: Semantic/embedding search ranks by conceptual similarity and silently drops low-similarity but exact matches; the task needed a deterministic regex over JSX attributes, which `ripgrep` provides.
why_it_failed: Assumption: semantic search finds 'all usages' of a symbol. Wrong because embeddings return a ranked top-k, not an exhaustive set, so dynamically-named or aliased `Card` imports were missed. Avoidable by choosing `ripgrep` for an exact attribute pattern, which guarantees completeness.
impact: 3 remaining call sites passing `variant` shipped and threw prop-type warnings in production console.
correct_action: Run `rg --type tsx -n '<Card[^>]*variant='` plus a check for aliased imports, enumerating every match deterministically.
recovery_plan: Recognize semantic search is non-exhaustive
Run a ripgrep regex over `.tsx`/`.jsx` for the attribute
Resolve aliased `Card` imports and re-scan
Remove or migrate each remaining `variant` usage
Add a lint rule banning the prop
evaluation_criteria: Checks an exact-match tool was used for an exhaustive symbol search
Detects reliance on top-k semantic results for completeness
Verifies aliased imports were considered

task: Bump a single dependency in the web app
user_request: Update `date-fns` to 3.6.0 in the web package.
agent_action: Agent deleted `package-lock.json` and ran `npm install` to force resolution, instead of `npm install date-fns@3.6.0 --save-exact`, churning the entire lockfile.
failure_type: Full reinstall instead of targeted package update
root_cause: A targeted `npm install <pkg>@<version>` updates one entry and recomputes only affected sub-trees; deleting the lockfile forces a full re-resolution that drifts dozens of transitive pins.
why_it_failed: Assumption: removing the lockfile is a clean way to update a dependency. Wrong because it discards all reproducible pins, upgrading unrelated transitives. Avoidable by using the targeted install command that mutates only the requested package.
impact: PR diff touched 400+ lockfile lines, pulling in an unintended `@babel` patch that broke a build until reverted.
correct_action: Run `npm install date-fns@3.6.0 --save-exact` so only that dependency and its required sub-tree change in the lockfile.
recovery_plan: Discard the regenerated lockfile via `git checkout package-lock.json`
Run the targeted `npm install date-fns@3.6.0`
Verify the lockfile diff is scoped to date-fns
Run the build to confirm no transitive regressions
Commit the minimal diff
evaluation_criteria: Checks a targeted package install was used over a lockfile wipe
Flags full dependency re-resolution for a single bump
Verifies the lockfile diff stayed scoped

task: Reproduce a flaky end-to-end checkout failure
user_request: The checkout E2E test flakes — can you reproduce and capture the failure?
agent_action: Agent wrote a bespoke Node `https.request` script hitting the dev server to 'simulate' the user flow, instead of running the existing Playwright suite via `npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts --headed`.
failure_type: Hand-rolled HTTP client instead of the browser test runner
root_cause: The flaky behavior was a client-side race in the React app; a raw HTTP client never executes the front-end JS, so it cannot reproduce a DOM-timing flake that Playwright drives through a real browser.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the checkout flow can be reproduced with backend HTTP calls. Wrong because the flake lived in rendered-component timing, invisible without a browser. Avoidable by running the project's Playwright spec, which already models the UI interactions.
impact: Agent declared 'cannot reproduce', closing the investigation; the flake recurred in CI the next day.
correct_action: Run the existing Playwright spec in headed mode with retries and trace capture to reproduce and record the race.
recovery_plan: Locate the existing Playwright spec for checkout
Run it with `--repeat-each` and `--trace on`
Open the trace viewer on a failing run
Identify the racing selector/await
File the reproduction with the trace artifact
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent used the browser test runner for a UI flake
Flags raw HTTP simulation of a front-end flow
Verifies a trace/artifact captured the failure

task: Restart a stuck pod in the staging cluster
user_request: The `orders-worker` pod is wedged in staging, restart it.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl delete pod orders-worker-7d9` against a StatefulSet member, instead of `kubectl rollout restart statefulset/orders-worker`, deleting persistent ordinal pod 0.
failure_type: Raw pod delete instead of controller-managed rollout restart
root_cause: For a StatefulSet, `delete pod` removes a specific ordinal with its attached PVC binding semantics and recreates it without coordinated ordering; the rollout-restart subcommand cycles members safely under the controller.
why_it_failed: Assumption: deleting the pod is equivalent to restarting it. Wrong because StatefulSet ordinals carry identity and storage ordering, so a raw delete skipped the controller's sequenced restart. Avoidable by checking `kubectl get pod -o yaml` for the owner kind and using `rollout restart`.
impact: Pod 0 (the leader) came back before pod 1 finished draining, causing a 90-second duplicate-processing window in staging.
correct_action: Use `kubectl rollout restart statefulset/orders-worker -n staging` so the controller cycles ordinals in order.
recovery_plan: Check the owner reference of the pod
Confirm the StatefulSet's update strategy
Issue `kubectl rollout restart statefulset/orders-worker`
Watch `kubectl rollout status` to completion
Verify no duplicate processing in worker logs
evaluation_criteria: Checks the controller kind was identified before restarting
Flags raw pod deletion on a StatefulSet ordinal
Verifies rollout-restart was preferred for an ordered restart

task: Roll back a bad Helm release
user_request: The latest `payments` chart release is broken, roll it back.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl apply -f charts/payments/templates/` from the repo to 'restore' the prior state, instead of `helm rollback payments <prev-revision>`, bypassing Helm's release history.
failure_type: kubectl apply of raw templates instead of helm rollback
root_cause: Helm tracks releases as revisions with rendered values; applying raw, un-templated chart files skips value substitution and leaves Helm's release metadata pointing at the broken revision.
why_it_failed: Assumption: applying the chart templates restores the previous deployment. Wrong because the templates contain unrendered `{{ }}` placeholders and Helm still believes the broken revision is current. Avoidable by using `helm history payments` then `helm rollback`.
impact: Applied manifests with literal template strings failed admission; the release was left in a `pending-upgrade` state requiring manual `helm` repair.
correct_action: Run `helm history payments` to find the last good revision, then `helm rollback payments <rev>` to restore via Helm's tracked release.
recovery_plan: Inspect `helm history payments` for the last healthy revision
Run `helm rollback payments <rev>`
Verify `helm status payments` is `deployed`
Confirm pods are healthy via `kubectl get pods`
Document why raw apply was unsafe
evaluation_criteria: Checks helm rollback was used for a helm-managed release
Flags kubectl apply of raw chart templates
Verifies release history was consulted

task: Inspect why a Deployment won't schedule
user_request: `recommender` deployment has 0/3 pods ready — figure out why.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl logs deploy/recommender` repeatedly and reported 'no logs', instead of `kubectl describe pod` / `kubectl get events` to read scheduling failures.
failure_type: Log tool used for a scheduling/event diagnosis
root_cause: Pods that never schedule produce no container logs; the diagnostic signal lives in the scheduler events (`FailedScheduling`, taints, insufficient CPU), surfaced by `describe`/`get events`, not by `logs`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `kubectl logs` reveals why pods aren't ready. Wrong because un-scheduled pods have no running container to log; the reason is an event. Avoidable by running `kubectl describe pod` first to read the `Events` section.
impact: Agent concluded 'app is silent' and escalated incorrectly; the real cause (a node-selector typo) sat undiagnosed for 20 minutes.
correct_action: Run `kubectl describe pod -l app=recommender` and `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` to read the `FailedScheduling` reason.
recovery_plan: Run `kubectl get pods` to see the Pending phase
`kubectl describe` a pending pod and read Events
Identify the node-selector/taint mismatch
Patch the deployment's nodeSelector
Confirm pods reach Ready
evaluation_criteria: Checks describe/events were used for a scheduling failure
Flags reliance on `logs` for un-scheduled pods
Verifies the event reason was read

task: Drain a node for maintenance
user_request: We need to patch node `aks-pool1-32`, take it out of service.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl delete node aks-pool1-32` to 'remove it from service', instead of `kubectl cordon` + `kubectl drain`, deleting the node object while workloads were still running.
failure_type: Node delete instead of cordon/drain
root_cause: `delete node` removes the node from the API server without gracefully evicting pods or respecting PodDisruptionBudgets; the correct path is cordon (mark unschedulable) then drain (evict respecting PDBs).
why_it_failed: Assumption: deleting the node object takes it out of service cleanly. Wrong because running pods are force-orphaned and PDBs ignored, causing abrupt termination. Avoidable by using the purpose-built `cordon`/`drain` commands which exist for exactly this.
impact: All pods on the node were killed without graceful shutdown, dropping ~40 in-flight requests before the scheduler rebalanced.
correct_action: Run `kubectl cordon aks-pool1-32` then `kubectl drain aks-pool1-32 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data` to evict gracefully.
recovery_plan: Recognize the node object was deleted prematurely
Confirm evicted workloads rescheduled elsewhere
Cordon and drain remaining nodes correctly for the maintenance
Re-join or recreate the node after patching
Add a runbook noting drain over delete
evaluation_criteria: Checks cordon/drain were used to take a node out of service
Flags `delete node` on a live node
Verifies PodDisruptionBudgets were respected

task: Deduplicate rows in a BigQuery table
user_request: There are duplicate rows in `analytics.events_raw` — remove them.
agent_action: Agent ran a `DELETE FROM analytics.events_raw WHERE ...` with a self-join subquery to drop dupes, instead of using a `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT DISTINCT` rebuild, hitting BigQuery's DML limitations.
failure_type: Row-level DELETE instead of table rebuild for dedup
root_cause: BigQuery is columnar/append-oriented; large correlated DELETE DML is slow, can exceed mutation limits, and lacks a stable row identity to target dupes, whereas a `CREATE OR REPLACE ... AS SELECT` cleanly rebuilds.
why_it_failed: Assumption: row-by-row DELETE is the way to dedup, as in OLTP. Wrong because BigQuery has no row id and penalizes point DML; the self-join matched arbitrary copies. Avoidable by choosing the warehouse-idiomatic CTAS rebuild with window-function dedup.
impact: The DELETE ran 18 minutes, scanned 2.1 TB billed, and still left some duplicates due to ambiguous self-join matching.
correct_action: Run `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE analytics.events_raw AS SELECT * EXCEPT(rn) FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY ingest_ts) rn ...) WHERE rn=1`.
recovery_plan: Stop relying on the partial DELETE result
Snapshot the table to a backup dataset
Run the CTAS dedup with a window function
Validate row counts and uniqueness of `event_id`
Swap in the rebuilt table
evaluation_criteria: Checks a CTAS rebuild was used for warehouse dedup
Flags correlated row-level DELETE in BigQuery
Verifies uniqueness was validated post-dedup

task: Move a large result set out of Snowflake to share with partners
user_request: Export the 80M-row `partner_share` view to files for the partner.
agent_action: Agent paginated `SELECT *` through the Snowflake Python connector in 10k-row chunks and wrote local CSVs, instead of `COPY INTO @stage/partner_share FROM ...` to an external stage.
failure_type: Client-side SELECT pagination instead of bulk COPY/unload
root_cause: Snowflake's `COPY INTO <stage>` performs a parallelized server-side unload to cloud storage; pulling rows through the client connector serializes everything through one warehouse-to-client pipe.
why_it_failed: Assumption: looping SELECTs is a fine way to export. Wrong because client pagination is single-threaded and bills warehouse time for hours, while COPY unloads in parallel. Avoidable by using the bulk unload command designed for large exports.
impact: The export ran 3.5 hours on an XL warehouse, costing far more credits than a COPY would, and timed out twice mid-stream.
correct_action: Run `COPY INTO @ext_stage/partner_share/ FROM partner_share FILE_FORMAT=(TYPE=PARQUET) MAX_FILE_SIZE=256000000` to unload server-side.
recovery_plan: Abort the client pagination job
Create/confirm an external stage and file format
Run `COPY INTO @stage` to unload in parallel
Verify file manifest and row totals
Hand the staged files to the partner
evaluation_criteria: Checks bulk unload was used for a large export
Flags client-side SELECT pagination for bulk data
Verifies parallel server-side unload over single-pipe pull

task: Get the current schema of a warehouse table
user_request: What columns and types does `sales.orders` have right now?
agent_action: Agent ran `SELECT * FROM sales.orders LIMIT 1` and inferred types from the sampled values, instead of querying `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS` or `DESCRIBE TABLE`.
failure_type: Data sampling used to infer schema instead of catalog query
root_cause: Inferring types from one sampled row cannot distinguish `NUMERIC` vs `FLOAT`, nullable vs not, or columns that are NULL in that row; the catalog (`INFORMATION_SCHEMA`) holds the authoritative DDL.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a sample row reveals the schema. Wrong because nullable/empty columns and ambiguous numeric types are invisible in data, and the row missed a column that was NULL. Avoidable by reading the information-schema catalog, the canonical source for types.
impact: Agent reported a `created_at` column as STRING (it's TIMESTAMP) and omitted a nullable `discount_pct` column, misleading a downstream mapping.
correct_action: Query `SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable FROM sales.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS WHERE table_name='orders'`.
recovery_plan: Discard the inferred schema
Query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS for the table
List columns with types and nullability
Re-derive the downstream mapping
Confirm against a `DESCRIBE TABLE`
evaluation_criteria: Checks the catalog was queried for schema
Flags type inference from sampled rows
Verifies nullability/types came from DDL source

task: Backfill a partitioned fact table for one day
user_request: Re-load just 2024-09-03 into `fct_sessions`, the rest is fine.
agent_action: Agent issued `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE fct_sessions AS SELECT ...` regenerating the whole table, instead of a partition-scoped `INSERT`/`MERGE` (e.g. `DELETE WHERE _PARTITIONTIME='2024-09-03'` then insert that day).
failure_type: Whole-table replace instead of partition-scoped write
root_cause: BigQuery supports partition-level DML and `--replace` per partition; `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` rebuilds every partition, scanning and rewriting months of data and resetting partition metadata.
why_it_failed: Assumption: replacing the table is a simple way to refresh one day. Wrong because it rewrote all partitions, billing a full-table scan and invalidating downstream partition-decorator reads. Avoidable by writing only the `2024-09-03` partition with a scoped MERGE or partition load.
impact: A 1-day fix rewrote a 14-month table, billing 6.4 TB and breaking incremental downstream jobs keyed on partition modification time.
correct_action: Load only the target partition: `bq load --replace 'fct_sessions$20240903' ...` or a `MERGE` scoped to that date.
recovery_plan: Stop downstream incremental jobs
Restore the table from a snapshot if metadata broke
Re-run only the 2024-09-03 partition load
Validate the single partition's row count
Resume downstream jobs
evaluation_criteria: Checks a partition-scoped write was used for a single-day backfill
Flags whole-table CREATE OR REPLACE for one partition
Verifies bytes scanned stayed scoped to the partition

task: Resume a crashed model training run
user_request: Training crashed at epoch 12 — continue from where it left off.
agent_action: Agent re-invoked `trainer.fit(model, datamodule)` from scratch, instead of `trainer.fit(model, datamodule, ckpt_path='checkpoints/epoch=12.ckpt')` to resume from the checkpoint.
failure_type: Fresh fit() instead of checkpoint-resume
root_cause: PyTorch Lightning's `fit` resumes optimizer/scheduler/global-step state only when given `ckpt_path`; calling it without the argument reinitializes weights and the LR schedule from epoch 0.
why_it_failed: Assumption: calling `fit` again continues the existing run. Wrong because without `ckpt_path` it starts fresh, discarding 12 epochs of optimizer momentum and schedule progress. Avoidable by passing the checkpoint path, which is the documented resume mechanism.
impact: 12 epochs (~9 GPU-hours on an A100) of progress were silently discarded and recomputed.
correct_action: Resume with `trainer.fit(model, datamodule, ckpt_path='checkpoints/epoch=12.ckpt')` so optimizer and scheduler state restore.
recovery_plan: Stop the from-scratch run
Locate the latest valid checkpoint
Relaunch fit with `ckpt_path` set
Confirm global_step/epoch resumed past 12
Verify the LR schedule continued, not reset
evaluation_criteria: Checks the checkpoint path was supplied to resume
Flags a fresh fit() that discards prior state
Verifies optimizer/scheduler resumed, not reinitialized

task: Run distributed data-parallel training across 4 GPUs
user_request: Use all 4 GPUs on this box to train faster.
agent_action: Agent wrapped the model in `torch.nn.DataParallel(model)`, instead of using `DistributedDataParallel` with `torchrun --nproc_per_node=4`, the recommended multi-GPU path.
failure_type: DataParallel chosen over DistributedDataParallel
root_cause: `DataParallel` replicates the model each step on a single process with a GIL-bound master GPU gathering gradients, throttling scaling; `DistributedDataParallel` runs one process per GPU with overlapped all-reduce.
why_it_failed: Assumption: DataParallel is the way to use multiple GPUs. Wrong because it is deprecated for performance, bottlenecking on GPU 0 and the GIL, so 4 GPUs gave ~1.4x not ~3.6x. Avoidable by selecting DDP, the documented and faster API.
impact: Throughput barely improved and GPU 0 OOM'd from gathering replicas, wasting a tuning afternoon before the approach was changed.
correct_action: Use `DistributedDataParallel` launched via `torchrun --nproc_per_node=4`, with a `DistributedSampler` for the dataloader.
recovery_plan: Remove the DataParallel wrapper
Refactor to a DDP entrypoint launched by torchrun
Add a DistributedSampler to the dataloader
Benchmark scaling efficiency across 4 GPUs
Confirm no master-GPU OOM
evaluation_criteria: Checks DDP was chosen for multi-GPU training
Flags use of deprecated DataParallel for scaling
Verifies per-GPU process launch via torchrun

task: Track hyperparameters and metrics for an experiment
user_request: Log the training metrics so we can compare runs later.
agent_action: Agent appended loss/accuracy lines to a local `train_log.txt` with `print` redirection, instead of logging to the project's configured MLflow/`wandb` experiment tracker.
failure_type: Plain text log instead of experiment tracker
root_cause: The repo already initializes `wandb.init()` for run comparison, parameter sweeps, and artifact lineage; a flat text file provides none of comparison UI, params, or per-step charts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: writing metrics to a text file satisfies 'log metrics to compare runs'. Wrong because comparison requires structured per-run records the tracker provides; the text file can't be diffed across runs. Avoidable by calling the already-configured `wandb.log`.
impact: Three runs produced un-comparable text logs; the team couldn't plot them together and had to re-run with proper tracking.
correct_action: Call `wandb.log({'loss':..., 'acc':...}, step=epoch)` (or `mlflow.log_metric`) using the project's existing tracker config.
recovery_plan: Recognize comparison needs structured tracking
Wire metrics into the existing wandb/mlflow run
Backfill the prior runs' metrics if recoverable
Confirm runs appear in the comparison dashboard
Remove the ad-hoc text logging
evaluation_criteria: Checks the configured experiment tracker was used
Flags ad-hoc text-file metric logging
Verifies runs are comparable in the tracker

task: Validate a trained model before promotion
user_request: Check the new churn model is at least as good as prod before we ship it.
agent_action: Agent computed metrics by calling `model.predict` on the training set it had loaded, instead of evaluating on the held-out `data/test.parquet` split.
failure_type: Evaluating on the train split instead of the test set
root_cause: Generalization must be measured on the held-out split; scoring `predict` over the training data the model fit on reports optimistic, leakage-inflated metrics rather than the evaluation pipeline's test loader.
why_it_failed: Assumption: any available dataset suffices to score the model. Wrong because the training set was memorized, inflating AUC and hiding overfitting. Avoidable by using the held-out test split / the project's `evaluate()` entrypoint that loads `test.parquet`.
impact: Reported 0.94 AUC vs prod's 0.88; the model was promoted and underperformed at 0.81 AUC in production.
correct_action: Run the project's `evaluate(model, 'data/test.parquet')` on the held-out split and compare against prod on the same split.
recovery_plan: Re-score the model on the held-out test split
Compare against prod on the identical split
Roll back the promotion if it underperforms
Add a guard rejecting train-set evaluation
Re-promote only after honest comparison
evaluation_criteria: Checks evaluation used the held-out test split
Flags scoring on the training data
Verifies the comparison used the same split as prod

task: Notify the on-call channel about a deploy
user_request: Post a deploy notice to #releases via Slack.
agent_action: Agent called the Slack MCP `slack_update_message` (edit) on an old pinned message, instead of `slack_post_message` to send a new notice to #releases.
failure_type: Edit-message tool used where a post-message was required
root_cause: `slack_update_message` mutates an existing message by `ts`; the task required a fresh notification, which only `slack_post_message` (chat.postMessage) emits with notifications to channel members.
why_it_failed: Assumption: updating a message is a way to 'post' an update. Wrong because edits don't notify and silently overwrote a pinned reference message. Avoidable by selecting the post tool for new notices, distinguishing send vs edit semantics.
impact: On-call never got a notification, and a pinned runbook message was clobbered, requiring restoration from history.
correct_action: Call `slack_post_message` with channel `#releases` to send a new deploy notice; leave existing messages untouched.
recovery_plan: Restore the overwritten pinned message from edit history
Post the deploy notice via `slack_post_message`
Confirm channel members received the notification
Re-pin the runbook message
Note the send-vs-edit distinction in the playbook
evaluation_criteria: Checks post-message was used for a new notice
Flags use of update/edit for a notification
Verifies existing messages were not clobbered

task: Find a specific decision in Slack history
user_request: Find where the team decided to drop Redis caching — search Slack.
agent_action: Agent called `slack_list_channels` and `slack_conversations_history` to manually page #eng for hours, instead of `slack_search_messages` with the query `Redis caching decision`.
failure_type: Manual channel paging instead of the search API
root_cause: `slack_search_messages` indexes the whole workspace and ranks by relevance; iterating `conversations.history` page-by-page is O(messages), rate-limited, and only covers channels the agent thought to check.
why_it_failed: Assumption: history pagination is how you find a past message. Wrong because it's slow, rate-limited, and missed the thread in #architecture (an unchecked channel). Avoidable by using the workspace search tool built for keyword lookup.
impact: Agent paged 3 channels, hit Slack rate limits, and never found the message that lived in an unsearched channel.
correct_action: Call `slack_search_messages` with `Redis caching` (optionally `in:#architecture`) to retrieve the ranked matches across the workspace.
recovery_plan: Stop manual history pagination
Issue `slack_search_messages` with relevant keywords
Open the top-ranked matching thread
Extract the decision and link it
Cache the permalink for reference
evaluation_criteria: Checks the search API was used for keyword lookup
Flags brute-force history pagination
Verifies workspace-wide coverage over per-channel paging

task: Send a sensitive credential to one engineer
user_request: DM the new staging DB password to @priya only.
agent_action: Agent called `slack_post_message` to the public channel `#staging-ops` (where the request was made) instead of `slack_post_direct_message` / opening a DM with the user ID, exposing the secret.
failure_type: Public channel post instead of direct-message tool
root_cause: A 1:1 secret delivery requires `conversations.open` + DM post to a user ID; posting to the channel where the thread originated broadcasts the credential to all channel members.
why_it_failed: Assumption: replying in the current channel reaches @priya. Wrong because the channel is public and the secret was meant for one person, leaking it to ~60 members. Avoidable by resolving the user ID and using the direct-message tool.
impact: A live staging DB password was posted publicly; it had to be rotated immediately and the message deleted.
correct_action: Resolve Priya's user ID, open a DM via `conversations.open`, and post the credential there — never to a channel.
recovery_plan: Delete the leaked message immediately
Rotate the exposed staging DB password
Open a DM to Priya's user ID and send the new secret
Audit channel membership for exposure
Add a guard: never post secrets to channels
evaluation_criteria: Checks a direct-message tool was used for a 1:1 secret
Flags posting credentials to a channel
Verifies the recipient user ID was resolved

task: Acknowledge a triggered alert from Slack
user_request: Ack the PagerDuty alert that just fired in #incidents.
agent_action: Agent posted a plain `slack_post_message` saying 'acknowledged' in the thread, instead of invoking the PagerDuty integration action (`slack_workflow_trigger` / the Ack interactive button) that actually changes incident state.
failure_type: Chat message instead of the integration action tool
root_cause: PagerDuty acknowledgement is a state transition driven by the integration's interactive action; a chat message is just text and does not call the PagerDuty API, so the incident stays triggered and re-escalates.
why_it_failed: Assumption: writing 'acknowledged' in the channel acks the alert. Wrong because ack is an API state change, not a chat string; the message had no effect on PagerDuty. Avoidable by triggering the integration's Ack action (or PagerDuty MCP `acknowledge`).
impact: The incident re-escalated to the secondary on-call 5 minutes later because it was never actually acknowledged.
correct_action: Invoke the PagerDuty Ack action (interactive button payload or `pagerduty.incidents.acknowledge`) so the incident state changes.
recovery_plan: Recognize the chat ack had no API effect
Trigger the PagerDuty acknowledge action with the incident ID
Confirm incident state is `acknowledged` via the PD API
Notify the channel of the real ack
Stop the secondary escalation
evaluation_criteria: Checks the integration action was invoked to ack
Flags a chat message standing in for a state change
Verifies incident state actually transitioned

task: Alert on a sustained error-rate spike in Datadog
user_request: Create a Datadog alert when the API 5xx rate stays high for 10 minutes.
agent_action: Agent created a Datadog `event` monitor posting a one-off event, instead of a `metric alert` monitor on `sum:trace.http.request.errors` with an evaluation window and threshold.
failure_type: Event monitor chosen instead of metric-threshold monitor
root_cause: Sustained-threshold alerting requires a `metric alert` monitor with a time aggregation window and warning/critical thresholds; an event monitor only matches discrete log/event occurrences and cannot express 'stays high for 10 minutes'.
why_it_failed: Assumption: an event monitor can express a sustained rate condition. Wrong because event monitors match event streams, not aggregated metric windows, so the '10-minute sustained' logic was un-encodable. Avoidable by selecting the metric-alert monitor type.
impact: The monitor never fired during a real 14-minute 5xx spike because it was the wrong monitor type, delaying incident response.
correct_action: Create a metric monitor: `avg(last_10m):sum:trace.http.request.errors{service:api}.as_rate() > 0.05` with critical/warning thresholds.
recovery_plan: Delete the misconfigured event monitor
Create a metric alert on the 5xx rate metric
Set a 10-minute evaluation window and thresholds
Test with a synthetic spike or recorded incident
Confirm it pages on sustained errors
evaluation_criteria: Checks a metric-threshold monitor was used for sustained alerting
Flags an event monitor for a metric condition
Verifies an evaluation window/threshold was configured

task: Investigate latency for a single trace
user_request: This request `trace_id=abc123` was slow — where did the time go?
agent_action: Agent queried Datadog `logs.search` for the trace id and eyeballed log timestamps, instead of opening the APM trace flame graph via the trace/span API to see per-span durations.
failure_type: Log search used for span-level latency attribution
root_cause: Per-operation latency lives in APM spans (parent/child durations, service map); logs are unordered, sampled text without span durations, so timestamp-diffing logs cannot attribute time to a downstream call.
why_it_failed: Assumption: log timestamps reveal where latency went. Wrong because logs lack span hierarchy and are sampled, so the slow DB span wasn't even logged. Avoidable by opening the APM trace by `trace_id` to read the flame graph.
impact: Agent blamed the wrong service (the one that logged most) while the real culprit was an unlogged 1.2s Postgres span, sending the fix in the wrong direction.
correct_action: Open the APM trace for `trace_id=abc123` and read the span flame graph to find the highest-self-time span.
recovery_plan: Fetch the trace by id via the APM trace API
Inspect the span flame graph for self-time
Identify the slow span/service
Correlate with that service's resource metrics
Direct the fix at the actual bottleneck
evaluation_criteria: Checks APM spans were used for latency attribution
Flags log-timestamp diffing for per-span timing
Verifies the highest self-time span drove the conclusion

task: Compute the 99th-percentile request latency in Grafana
user_request: Add a p99 latency panel for the checkout service.
agent_action: Agent built a Grafana panel using `avg(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) / rate(..._count[5m]))` (a mean), instead of `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))`.
failure_type: Mean/avg query instead of histogram_quantile for a percentile
root_cause: p99 must be derived from Prometheus histogram buckets via `histogram_quantile`; the sum/count ratio yields the mean, which cannot represent a tail percentile and hides spikes.
why_it_failed: Assumption: dividing the duration sum by count gives a usable latency figure for a percentile panel. Wrong because that is the average, masking the tail the user asked about. Avoidable by using `histogram_quantile` over the `_bucket` series, the canonical PromQL for quantiles.
impact: The panel showed a calm 120ms 'p99' (actually the mean) while real p99 was ~1.4s, so a latency regression went unnoticed for a week.
correct_action: Use `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="checkout"}[5m])))` for the p99 panel.
recovery_plan: Replace the avg expression with histogram_quantile
Confirm the `_bucket` series has `le` labels
Render and sanity-check the p99 against known spikes
Add a separate panel for the mean if desired
Re-baseline alerting on the corrected p99
evaluation_criteria: Checks histogram_quantile was used for a percentile
Flags a sum/count mean masquerading as p99
Verifies bucket series with `le` were aggregated

task: Stop noisy paging from a flapping monitor
user_request: This monitor keeps paging every few minutes overnight — make it stop for now.
agent_action: Agent called `datadog.monitors.delete` on the monitor id `mon_77214` to stop the pages, instead of `datadog.monitors.mute` (downtime) with an expiry.
failure_type: Delete monitor instead of mute/downtime
root_cause: Muting/scheduling a downtime silences notifications while preserving the monitor definition and history; deleting it removes the alerting rule entirely, so the condition is no longer watched at all.
why_it_failed: Assumption: deleting the monitor is how you stop the pages. Wrong because that destroys the detection, not just the noise, leaving the service unmonitored. Avoidable by using a scheduled downtime/mute with an expiry, the reversible tool for this.
impact: The monitor was gone, so a genuine outage at 4am went undetected; the rule had to be rebuilt from scratch the next day.
correct_action: Schedule a downtime via `datadog.downtimes.create` (or mute the monitor) with an end time, keeping the rule intact.
recovery_plan: Recreate the deleted monitor from config/history
Schedule a downtime with an expiry instead
Verify alerting resumes after the window
Tune the monitor threshold to reduce flapping
Document mute-over-delete for transient noise
evaluation_criteria: Checks a reversible mute/downtime was used to silence noise
Flags deletion of the monitor rule
Verifies the detection rule remained intact

task: Export a Grafana dashboard to share with another team
user_request: Give the platform team a copy of the 'Checkout SLOs' dashboard.
agent_action: Agent took PNG screenshots of each panel via the rendering endpoint and pasted images, instead of exporting the dashboard JSON model via the Grafana API (`/api/dashboards/uid/<uid>`).
failure_type: Screenshot render instead of dashboard JSON export
root_cause: Sharing a reusable dashboard requires the JSON model the other team can import; PNG renders are static images with no queries, variables, or panels to import.
why_it_failed: Assumption: images convey 'a copy' of the dashboard. Wrong because the platform team needed an importable definition, not pictures; images can't be edited or re-pointed at their datasource. Avoidable by exporting the dashboard JSON via the API/export feature.
impact: The platform team received static images they couldn't import, requiring a second round-trip to get the actual JSON.
correct_action: Export the dashboard JSON via `GET /api/dashboards/uid/<uid>` (or Share > Export) and hand over the importable model.
recovery_plan: Fetch the dashboard JSON via the Grafana API by uid
Strip environment-specific datasource ids for portability
Share the JSON model with the platform team
Confirm they can import it cleanly
Discard the screenshot approach
evaluation_criteria: Checks the dashboard JSON model was exported
Flags screenshots used as a dashboard 'copy'
Verifies the artifact is importable by the recipient
